newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FOCUS-Pakistan's Engro sees further growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Pakistan's Engro sees further growth.

text.p: Engro Chemical Pakistan Ltd, a highly profitable fertiliser producer, is intent on diversifying, its chairman Shaukat Mirza says.
"Our vision is to become a diversified chemical company operating internationally," he told Reuters in an interview.

Mirza, who is also president and chief executive, said Engro had grown substantially in the last six years and had implemented or was developing projects worth $275 million directly or through joint ventures.
"As a result, earnings have grown rapidly during this period," he said. "The company has a sound business strategy for continued growth and diversification."
Analysts regard Engro as one of Pakistan's best blue chips because of its track record of mounting profits and dividends.
"We expect compounded average growth in earnings of about 30 percent in the next two years," an analyst at ING Barings said.

Engro's after-tax profit soared 77 percent to 1.386 billion rupees ($34.5 million) in calendar 1996 from 783 million rupees in 1995 on growth in urea fertiliser sales to 7.168 billion rupees last year from 4.52 billion rupees in 1995.
It paid out 25 percent bonus stocks and an 80 percent cash dividend for 1996 compared to 20 percent bonus stocks and a 60 percent dividend for 1995.
Engro, with listed paid-up capital of 700 million rupees, had reserves of 2.704 billion rupees at end-1996 compared to 2.008 billion in 1995.
An analyst at Taurus Securities said Engro's earnings per share was likely to rise 23 percent to 23.03 rupees in 1997, and 26.6 percent to 29.2 rupees in 1998.
"Engro Chemical is one of the top blue chip companies of Pakistan," an analyst at Kausar Abbas Bhayani Securities said.

Engro emerged in its present form in 1991, when the current management, employees and shareholders bought a 75 percent stake held by Exxon Corp of the United States, which had set up the company in Pakistan in the mid-1960s.
Foreign shareholders include the International Finance Corporation and the Commonwealth Development Corporation.

Engro launched a $120 million expansion plan in 1993, relocating an idle plant from the United States to Daharki in the southern province of Sindh in 1994. The plant, now 25 years old, added production capacity of 330,000 tonnes a year.
The government fixed Engro's gas feedstock price for 10 years from 1991. An eight-year tax holiday for the extra production from plant expansion expires in 2001.

Mirza said Engro was now engaged on a $59 million expansion at the Daharki plant to raise capacity to 850,000 tonnes by March 1998 from a current 750,000. Capacity could be further expanded to 1.2 million tonnes by the year 2000, he added.

The company is also working on the $65 million Engro Paktank Terminal Ltd (EPTL) project in Port Qasim, a joint venture with Royal Pakhoed of The Netherlands. Construction of a jetty and chemical terminal is expected to be completed by September 1997.
"A long-term usage agreement was successfully concluded between EPTL and ICI (Pakistan) to handle feedstock requirements of the ICI's PTA (pure terephthalic acid) project," Mirza said.
The $450 million PTA plant near Karachi, with a capacity of 400,000 tonnes a year, is due to come onstream by November.

Engro has also signed a memorandum of understanding with Mitsubishi Corporation and Asahi Glass Company of Japan to build a polyvinyl chloride (PVC) resin plant at Port Qasim, near Karachi, as part of its petrochemical complex.
"The PVC project, with an initial capacity of 100,000 tonnes per annum, is expected to be onstream during 1999 at an estimated cost of $80 million," Mirza said.

Engro's urea sales rose to 740,000 tonnes in 1996, a seven percent rise over 1995. It also sold 161,000 tonnes of imported urea, out of total urea imports of 700,000 tonnes, and boosted its market share to 23 percent from 21 percent in 1995.
"The demand for urea in 1996 grew by an impressive 17 percent over the previous year and reached 3.9 million tonnes," Mirza said.
